parts.text: The Word was with God and was God from the beginning; all things were made through him. He is the light and life of people, yet the world and his own people did not receive him. Those who believe on his name receive power to become the sons of God, born of God. The Word becomes flesh and reveals the Father’s glory, full of grace and truth. John witnesses to this light, denying that he is the Christ and identifying himself as the wilderness voice preparing the Lord’s way.

John calls Jesus the Lamb of God who takes away the world’s sin and testifies that the Spirit remained on him, identifying him as God’s Son. Andrew follows Jesus and brings Simon, whom Jesus names Cephas. Jesus calls Philip, who brings Nathanael. Jesus’ knowledge of Nathanael leads him to confess the Son of God and King of Israel, and Jesus promises greater things.

chapters.title: Wine at Cana and the temple cleansed

parts.text: At a wedding in Cana, Jesus’ mother tells him the wine has run out. He directs servants to fill six stone waterpots and take some to the feast’s governor. The water has become wine, and the governor praises its quality without knowing its source. This first miracle manifests Jesus’ glory, and his disciples believe on him. He then spends a short time in Capernaum with his family and disciples.

At passover in Jerusalem, Jesus drives merchants and animals from the temple and overturns the money changers’ tables, rejecting the treatment of his Father’s house as a marketplace. Challenged for a sign, he speaks of raising the destroyed temple in three days, meaning his body; his disciples understand after the resurrection. Many believe because of his miracles, but Jesus does not entrust himself to them, knowing what is within people.

chapters.title: New birth and faith in the Son

parts.text: Nicodemus visits Jesus at night. Jesus explains that seeing God’s kingdom requires being born again, of water and the Spirit, rather than merely natural birth. As Moses lifted up the serpent, the Son of man must be lifted up so believers may have eternal life. God gives his only begotten Son out of love for the world, bringing salvation rather than condemnation. Unbelief remains condemned; people avoid the light because their deeds are evil, while those who practice truth come to it.

When John’s disciples report that people are going to Jesus, John rejoices as the bridegroom’s friend. He is not the Christ and must decrease while Christ increases. The one from heaven speaks God’s words and has all things entrusted to him by the Father. Belief in the Son brings everlasting life; unbelief leaves a person under God’s wrath.

chapters.title: Living water and a healing word

parts.text: At Jacob’s well in Samaria, Jesus asks a woman for water and offers her living water springing up to everlasting life. He reveals knowledge of her five husbands and present relationship, leading her to recognize him as a prophet. Jesus says true worship will not depend on either her mountain or Jerusalem: the Father seeks worship in spirit and truth. When she mentions the coming Messias, Jesus identifies himself as that one.

The woman invites her town to meet Jesus. He tells the disciples that doing his Father’s will sustains him and that the fields are ready for harvest. Many Samaritans believe, first through her testimony and then through hearing Jesus themselves, recognizing the Savior of the world. Back in Galilee, a nobleman trusts Jesus’ word that his dying son lives. Learning that the fever left at that very hour, he and his household believe.

At Bethesda, Jesus heals a man disabled for thirty-eight years and tells him to carry his bed. Opposition arises because this happens on the sabbath and because Jesus calls God his Father, making himself equal with God. Jesus explains that the Son acts in harmony with the Father, gives life, and exercises judgment. Those hearing his word and believing the Father have everlasting life. All in the graves will hear his voice and rise, to life or condemnation.

Jesus says his judgment is just because he seeks his Father’s will. John bore witness to him, but his works, the Father, and the Scriptures provide greater testimony. His opponents search the Scriptures yet refuse to come to the one they testify about. Seeking honor from one another prevents belief; even Moses, whom they trust, wrote of him and will accuse their unbelief.

Jesus feeds about five thousand men with a boy’s five barley loaves and two fishes, leaving twelve baskets of fragments. He withdraws when they intend to make him king, then walks across the sea to his disciples. When the crowd follows, he directs them beyond perishable food to belief in the one God sent. He calls himself the bread of life, promising to receive those who come and raise believers at the last day.

His claim to have come from heaven provokes objections. Jesus says the Father draws people to him and that the bread he gives is his flesh for the world’s life. He speaks of eating his flesh and drinking his blood to have life, and explains that the Spirit gives life and his words are spirit and life. Many disciples leave. Peter affirms that Jesus has the words of eternal life, though Jesus identifies a betrayer among the twelve.

Jesus’ unbelieving brothers urge him to display himself publicly, but he acts according to his own appointed time and later goes quietly to the feast of tabernacles. Teaching in the temple, he says his doctrine comes from the Father and calls for righteous judgment rather than appearances, including about healing on the sabbath. People debate his identity and origin. Attempts to seize him fail because his hour has not come, and he speaks of returning to the one who sent him.

On the feast’s last day, Jesus invites the thirsty to come and drink, promising rivers of living water to believers; John explains that he means the Spirit they will receive after his glorification. The crowd remains divided over whether he is the Prophet or Christ. Officers return without arresting him, struck by his words. Nicodemus calls for a lawful hearing, but the other leaders dismiss him.

Scribes and Pharisees try to trap Jesus with a woman caught in adultery. He tells the sinless accuser to cast the first stone; convicted by conscience, they leave. He does not condemn her and commands her to sin no more. Declaring himself the light of the world, Jesus speaks of his Father’s witness, his heavenly origin, and the danger of dying in unbelief. He says his lifting up will reveal who he is and that he always does what pleases the Father.

Jesus promises freedom through truth to those continuing in his word. His hearers appeal to Abraham, but he exposes slavery to sin and contrasts Abraham’s conduct with their desire to kill him. Their lies and murderous intentions reflect the devil rather than God. He promises life to those keeping his word and declares, ‘Before Abraham was, I am.’ His opponents take up stones, but he leaves the temple.

chapters.title: A blind man sees and believes

parts.text: Seeing a man blind from birth, Jesus rejects the proposed explanation that his blindness resulted from his own or his parents’ sin, and says God’s works will be displayed in him. Jesus applies clay to his eyes and sends him to wash at Siloam; he returns seeing. Neighbors and Pharisees question him, with division arising because the healing occurred on the sabbath. His parents confirm his identity and former blindness but avoid further testimony for fear of expulsion from the synagogue.

The healed man refuses to deny what happened and argues that such a work points to someone from God. The leaders insult him and cast him out. Jesus finds him and identifies himself as the Son of God; the man believes and worships. Jesus contrasts those receiving sight with those claiming to see while remaining guilty, applying the warning to questioning Pharisees.

Jesus describes sheep recognizing their shepherd’s voice and rejecting strangers. He calls himself the door through which they enter for salvation and pasture, and the good shepherd who gives his life for them. Unlike a hired servant who flees danger, he knows and protects his own. He will bring other sheep into one fold under one shepherd. His death is voluntary, and he has authority to take up his life again. These words divide his hearers.

At the feast of dedication, Jesus points to his works as testimony and says his sheep hear his voice, follow him, and receive eternal life, secure in his and the Father’s hands. His declaration that he and the Father are one brings a charge of blasphemy. Appealing to Scripture and his works, he urges recognition that the Father is in him. He escapes arrest and goes beyond Jordan, where many believe.

Jesus hears that Lazarus is ill but remains two days before returning toward Judea, despite the danger there. He tells the disciples plainly that Lazarus has died. Arriving after four days in the grave, he assures Martha that her brother will rise and declares himself the resurrection and the life. Martha confesses him as Christ and God’s Son. Mary also comes grieving, and Jesus is deeply moved and weeps.

At the tomb, Jesus orders the stone removed, thanks the Father, and calls Lazarus out. Lazarus emerges still wrapped in graveclothes, and many witnesses believe. The leaders fear the consequences of Jesus’ growing following. Caiaphas says one man should die for the people; John explains that he unknowingly prophesies Jesus’ death for the nation and the gathering of God’s scattered children. They resolve to kill Jesus, who withdraws to Ephraim as passover approaches.

chapters.title: The king’s arrival and approaching death

parts.text: At Bethany, Mary anoints Jesus’ feet with costly ointment. Judas objects under the pretense of caring for the poor, though he is a thief; Jesus connects her act with his burial. The chief priests plan to kill Lazarus too because his restoration draws people to belief. The next day, crowds welcome Jesus with palm branches as Israel’s king. He rides a young ass, fulfilling Scripture that the disciples understand later.

When Greeks seek Jesus, he announces that his hour has come and compares his death to a grain of wheat producing fruit. A heavenly voice answers his prayer for the Father’s glory. He speaks of being lifted up, drawing people to himself, and urges belief in the light. Despite miracles, many remain unbelieving, fulfilling Esaias’s words; some believing rulers stay silent to preserve human approval. Jesus says his Father’s words bring life and will judge those rejecting them.

chapters.title: Serving, betrayal, and a new commandment

parts.text: Knowing his departure is near, Jesus washes his disciples’ feet. Peter first refuses, then asks for more washing when Jesus says it is necessary to have a part with him. Jesus explains their cleansing, while distinguishing the betrayer. As their Lord and Master, he has given an example of humble service that they should follow. He also foretells betrayal in fulfillment of Scripture, so its occurrence will strengthen their belief.

Jesus identifies the betrayer to the beloved disciple by giving Judas a dipped morsel. Satan enters Judas, who leaves into the night, though the others misunderstand his errand. Jesus speaks of his glorification and approaching departure, then commands the disciples to love one another as he has loved them; this will identify them as his followers. Peter promises to lay down his life, but Jesus predicts three denials before the cock crows.

chapters.title: The way to the Father and the promised Comforter

parts.text: Jesus comforts the disciples with his promise to prepare a place in his Father’s house and return to receive them. Answering Thomas, he declares himself the way, truth, and life, the only way to the Father. Answering Philip, he says that seeing him reveals the Father, who works through him. He promises works through believers and answers to requests in his name, bringing glory to the Father.

Love for Jesus is shown by keeping his commandments. He promises another Comforter, the Spirit of truth, who will remain with them and be in them. Jesus will not leave them comfortless; the Father and Son will dwell with those who love and obey him. The Holy Ghost will teach and recall his words. Jesus leaves them his peace and prepares them for his departure, acting in obedience to his Father.

Jesus is the true vine, his Father the husbandman, and the disciples branches that must abide in him to bear fruit. Fruitless branches are removed, fruitful ones are pruned, and branches apart from him wither. Abiding in his word and love involves obedience and brings joy. He commands mutual love like his own, whose greatest expression is laying down one’s life for friends. He calls them friends, shares the Father’s words, and appoints them to lasting fruitfulness.

Jesus warns that the world will hate his disciples because it first hated him and because they no longer belong to it. Servants can expect the treatment given their master. His words and works expose the guilt of those rejecting both him and the Father, fulfilling Scripture about causeless hatred. The coming Spirit of truth will testify of Jesus, and the disciples must also bear witness as those who have been with him.

Jesus warns his disciples that they will be expelled from synagogues and killed by people imagining they serve God. He tells them beforehand so persecution will not overthrow their faith. His departure will bring the Comforter, who will reprove the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment: unbelief in Jesus, his return to the Father, and the judgment of this world’s prince. The Spirit will guide the disciples into truth, reveal things to come, and glorify Jesus.

The disciples are puzzled by his promise that they will soon not see him, then see him again. Jesus compares their coming sorrow and joy to childbirth’s anguish followed by gladness. He encourages prayer to the Father in his name and assures them of the Father’s love. Though they profess belief, they will scatter and leave him; the Father remains with him. They may have peace in him despite tribulation, for he has overcome the world.

Jesus asks the Father to glorify him with the glory they shared before the world existed, having completed his given work and revealed the Father’s name. He describes eternal life as knowing the Father and Jesus Christ whom he sent. Praying for the disciples entrusted to him, he asks that they be kept united, protected from evil, filled with joy, and sanctified through God’s truthful word. They remain in a hostile world as those he sends into it.

Jesus also prays for future believers who will receive the disciples’ testimony. He asks that they be one in the Father and Son, so the world may recognize his mission and the Father’s love. He desires that his people be with him and behold the glory grounded in the Father’s love before creation. He will continue making the Father known, so that divine love and his own presence may dwell in them.

Judas leads an armed company to the garden, where Jesus openly identifies himself and secures his disciples’ release. Peter cuts off Malchus’s ear, but Jesus orders him to put away the sword and accepts the cup his Father has given. Bound, Jesus is taken first to Annas, then to Caiaphas. Questioned about his teaching, he points to its public character and challenges an officer who strikes him. Meanwhile Peter denies being his disciple three times, and the cock crows.

The leaders bring Jesus to Pilate while avoiding the judgment hall to preserve their ceremonial cleanness for passover. Pilate questions him about kingship. Jesus says his kingdom is not of this world; otherwise his servants would fight. He came to bear witness to truth, and those of the truth hear him. Pilate finds no fault and offers to release him, but the crowd demands Barabbas instead.

Pilate has Jesus scourged, and soldiers mock him with thorns and a purple robe. Though Pilate repeatedly finds no fault, the accusers demand death because Jesus claims to be God’s Son and pressure Pilate through loyalty to Cesar. Jesus says Pilate’s authority comes from above. Pilate yields, and Jesus is crucified at Golgotha between two others beneath a title naming him King of the Jews.

Soldiers divide Jesus’ clothes and cast lots for his coat, fulfilling Scripture. Jesus entrusts his mother to the beloved disciple, receives vinegar, declares that it is finished, and dies. Because he is already dead, soldiers do not break his legs, but one pierces his side and blood and water emerge. John presents these as witnessed fulfillments of Scripture. Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus wrap Jesus’ body with spices and place it in a nearby unused garden tomb.

chapters.title: The risen Lord and believing witnesses

parts.text: Mary Magdalene finds the stone removed and reports that Jesus’ body is missing. Peter and the beloved disciple inspect the empty tomb and its linen clothes. Mary remains weeping, sees two angels, and then encounters Jesus, initially mistaking him for the gardener. When he calls her by name, she recognizes him. He sends her to tell his brethren of his coming ascent to the Father, and she announces that she has seen the Lord.

Jesus appears to the disciples behind closed doors, shows his wounds, commissions them, and breathes on them to receive the Holy Ghost, speaking of remitting and retaining sins. Thomas is absent and demands physical evidence. Eight days later Jesus invites him to examine his wounds; Thomas confesses him as Lord and God. Jesus blesses those who believe without seeing. John explains that the recorded signs are written to bring belief and life in Jesus’ name.

chapters.title: Breakfast by the sea and Peter’s commission

parts.text: Seven disciples fish through the night without success. At dawn, the unrecognized Jesus tells them from shore to cast their net on the right, producing a great catch. The beloved disciple recognizes the Lord, and Peter jumps into the water to reach him. The others bring the boat and net, containing 153 large fish without breaking. Jesus has bread and fish ready and gives them breakfast, in his third appearance to the gathered disciples after rising.

Jesus asks Peter three times whether he loves him, and each time commissions him to feed his lambs or sheep. He foretells the death by which Peter will glorify God and commands him to follow. When Peter asks about the beloved disciple, Jesus redirects him to his own calling. John corrects the resulting rumor that this disciple would never die and affirms the truth of his testimony, while acknowledging that Jesus did far more than the book records.
